extracted.intended_audience: young ladies learning to ride / female equestrians (side-saddle)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical manual teaching young women how to ride side-saddle: selection and conformation of a lady's horse, personal and horse equipment, mounting and dismounting, rein management, seat and balance, paces, road etiquette, and handling vices/corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equestrian technicalities / terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Know and use the standard names for parts of the horse, bridle, and saddle (e.g., fore pastern, fetlock, arm, hock, stifle, haunch, crest, withers, croup; double head-stall, nose-band, throat-lash, snaffle rein, curb rein, martingale; near crutch, off crutch, cantle, crupper, skirt, stirrup, girths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few, among the most generally adopted, of these, it will be expedient, in the first place, to notice and explain. Knowing the proper names is presented as foundational; the manual illustrates parts and uses the terms throughout instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete lady's horse (overall ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'beau ideal' of the lady's horse: superlatively elegant in form, exquisitely fine in coat, unexceptionably beautiful in colour, height appropriate to the rider, graceful, accurate, well-united, thoroughly safe in every pace, 'light as a feather' in the hand but not painfully sensitive, bold yet superlatively docile, free from 'vice', excellent temper but not dull, rarely needing the whip yet responsive to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the composite ideal to aim for when selecting a horse for a lady; the manual emphasizes it is difficult to procure and often price is a consideration. Use this description as the checklist for an ideal mount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformation and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred conformation: small neat head well-set on an arched muscular neck; wide nostrils; large brilliant eyes; erect tapering ears; narrow elevated shoulder ridge; full fleshy chest; broad back; round/barrel-like body; long space between hips and tail with high-based tail on croup; distant fore and hind limbs; muscular arms; broad knees; wide hocks; flat sinewy legs; rather long pasterns; large nearly round hoofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual lists desirable physical traits in detail as evaluative criteria when judging a horse's suitability for a lady: these traits relate to style, soundness, comfort to rider, and safety in paces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coat condition, mane and tail grooming
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-bred, healthy, properly groomed horse should have a smooth, brilliantly polished coat; a rough or 'staring' coat considerably deteriorates appearance. Mane too long/thick interferes with delicate rein management; tail of immoderate length can be inconvenient by whisking to the sides; neither should be ungracefully brief or scanty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grooming and appropriate mane/tail length are explicitly included as part of the horse's suitability — anti-patterns include rough coat, overlong mane/tail, or excessively cropped appendages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour preferences and faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred colours: bright bay (with black mane/tail/lower legs) is most elegant; small white star or a white speck on a heel are beauties. Chestnut acceptable (but not with white legs). Certain greys (silver grey with black mane/tail) highly prized. Brown is less desirable; deep black can be elegant. Colours to avoid: roan, sorrel, dun, piebald, mouse, cream for everyday lady's horse; much white on face or legs is undesirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour is treated as an aesthetic criterion and a factor in taste; the manual gives a ranking and explicit colours to eschew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Height in proportion to rider
rubrics_metrics.description: The horse's height should harmonize with the rider's figure. A very young or short lady appears false on a lofty steed, and a tall woman is out of place on a diminutive pony. For ladies of general stature, a horse measuring from fifteen to fifteen and a half hands at the shoulder is usually most desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose height to produce graceful proportions; mismatch is an explicit anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paces (walk, canter, trot, hand-gallop) expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: A lady's horse should be perfect in paces (especially walk and canter): the walk should be fast, bold, firm, lively and steady; the canter light, easy, well-combined, graceful; the hand-gallop should be light and well-borne (though rarely used). The trot is less practised but an ideal lady's horse should perform it precisely with little concussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual prescribes which paces are prioritized for comfort and elegance; suitability in these paces is a key selection criterion. Anti-pattern: unsteady walk, heavy trot causing concussion to rider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament and mouth sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The horse should be bold yet docile, free from vice, excellent in temper but not dull; the mouth should be responsive to delicate hints of the bit — neither pulling hard nor being so tender as to suffer from moderate pressure. A horse that pulls or hangs on the reins is unsuitable; an overly tender mouth is also unsuitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combines behavioral and tack-response criteria. The manual emphasizes a balance: sensitive enough to subtle cues but not reactive or heavy-handed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal equipment: habit fit and style
rubrics_metrics.description: The riding habit should fit the bust without a crease; below the waist it ought to be long, somewhat full and flowing; its colour should be as dark as possible without being black. All that is gaudy, needless, or elaborate is vulgar; perfect simplicity in costume and trappings is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress is treated as etiquette and functional: avoid over-decoration; keep silhouette appropriate for side-saddle and dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hair and headgear
rubrics_metrics.description: Hair should be plaited or arranged & secured so it will not be blown into the eyes or discomposed by exercise/weather. Riding in a bonnet is inadvisable; a hat or neat undress military cap is indispensable and must be carefully secured. The veil is acceptable if moderate length and safely tied to the hat or cap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headgear and hair management are safety and etiquette concerns; anti-patterns include loose hair or insecure bonnets which might fall and startle the horse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whip: appearance and carriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The whip should be exquisitely neat and highly finished but with little, if any, decoration. It may be carried in the right hand with the lash downward between two fingers and the thumb or held like gentlemen; ensure the point does not tickle or irritate the horse's flank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whip is both a functional aid and a fashion accessory; neatness without ostentation is emphasized, and improper carriage that irritates the horse is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse accoutrements: simplicity and rejection of ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject ornamental trappings beyond the saddle and bridle as bad taste. Crupper and breast-band nearly obsolete; saddle-cloth nearly disappeared; nettings generally abandoned; martingale rarely seen. Simplicity is imperatively enjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual prescribes a minimalist tack approach for female equestrianism; ornate or excessive trappings are explicitly discouraged as vulgar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of the road and passing etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: On public roads: when proceeding in opposite directions, each party keeps to his/her near (left) side; when on parallel courses, the faster passes on the off (right). When meeting, a rider should take ground on the near/left; when passing slower traffic in same direction, take the off/right. When riding with a gentleman, there is etiquette whether the gentleman rides left or right of the lady (discussed with pros/cons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual gives explicit prescriptions for which side to take when meeting or overtaking, and considerations for riding beside a gentleman (e.g., which side better for giving assistance or avoiding soiling the lady's habit). Follow these rules to avoid danger and inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mounting procedure (side-saddle) and assistant duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach on the near side with skirt gathered up and whip in right hand. Groom gathers reins (curb tighter than bridoon), divides them with fore-finger. Lady receives reins slightly forward with right hand, passes whip over saddle to off side, places fore-finger between reins, takes near crutch with right hand and stands close to near side with back almost turned. Assistant steadies: the lady puts left foot in his hand, left hand on his shoulder, straightens left knee, rises perpendicularly, assistant raises her to be seated; assistant may use both hands if inexperienced. After seated, left foot placed in stirrup briefly, then returns to take seat with right knee between crutches. Keep reins light on bit during the process and do not put foot forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step-by-step directions with fingers of reins, hand placement, balance cues, and warnings (e.g., keep foot directly under when rising, assistant should not raise until weight is fully in his hand). Anti-patterns: improper foot placement, loose reins causing horse to move, assistant raising too early, hanging by crutch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groom handling of reins during mounting
rubrics_metrics.description: The groom should gather up the reins smoothly with his left hand, the curb rein between and somewhat tighter than the bridoon, dividing them with his fore-finger; then remove his hand so the lady draws them herself and keeps a light steady bearing on the bit while mounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit duty of the assistant to keep the horse steady and ensure safety during mounting; failing to hold the reins properly risks the horse moving and causing a mishap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rein handling and signals (two-hand then left-hand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginners hold reins separated, one in each hand, passed between 3rd/4th fingers, ends over fore-fingers, thumbs closed on them, hands level ~3 inches from body. Advanced riders hold both reins in left hand (various finger separations used, common: fourth & little finger), off rein over fourth, near under it; reins carried flat through hand near middle joint of fore-finger with thumb uppermost. Signal to advance: bring thumb towards self to slacken reins; to turn left: thumb to right little finger to left and back of hand up (left rein slackens, right tightens); to turn right: reverse motions; to stop/back: nails turned upwards, knuckles reversed, wrist rounded. Elbow should be neither squeezed nor thrust out; hand position and wrist posture specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed mechanical instructions for rein-holding and the subtle hand movements for forward, turn, and stop. Anti-patterns include incorrect finger positioning, squeezing elbows, or improper wrist posture producing crude signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seat and balance (posture and harmony with paces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Body must preserve balance and maintain seat; avoid hanging by the near crutch (which inclines body left, bends neck awkwardly, elevates right shoulder); harmonize movements with the horse's paces (rise/descend/advance/stop with, not after, the animal). Sit so weight rests on centre of saddle; shoulders even; do not bear weight on stirrup or hang on crutch; incline partially backward (not forward); head in natural position; chest advanced; shoulders thrown back; elbows steady; lower arm at right angle to upper; hands positioned as prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual emphasizes elegance, safety, and command derived from correct carriage and synchrony with the horse. Corrective guidance is given for common faults (see common errors). Anti-patterns: leaning forward, weight on stirrup, asymmetric shoulders, hanging on crutch, being tossed by paces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common errors and corrective guidance (hanging, asymmetry, timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common faults: hanging by the near crutch, inclining body to left, head bent right, right shoulder elevated, left depressed, sitting carelessly not in centre, taking weight on stirrup, rising after the animal. Corrections: sit with weight on centre of saddle, keep shoulders even, do not bear weight on stirrup, synchronize rise/descend/advance/stop with the horse, lean slightly backward to bring shoulders in and keep weight correctly borne.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit identification of common anti-patterns with concrete corrective posture and timing cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stirrup usage (limited role for side-saddle riders)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stirrup is of very little use except t... (manual begins to state the limited utility of the stirrup for side-saddle riders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context indicates stirrups should not be relied upon for bearing weight in ordinary seat; the manual discourages dependence on stirrup except for particular movements (e.g., mounting adjustments). Avoid placing persistent weight on stirrup as a postural crutch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aids, defences, soothings, animations, corrections, and vices (horse management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections (AIDS AND DEFENCES; SOOTHINGS AND ANIMATIONS; CORRECTIONS; VICES) indicate instruction covers how to apply aids (whip, reins), how to soothe and animate the horse, how to correct faults and manage vices. Vices should be recognized and the rider given methods to correct or avoid them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although detailed text is in later sections, the manual treats these as distinct practical evaluation/response categories: know appropriate aids, humane corrective measures, signs/management of vices, and methods to encourage or restrain the horse. Anti-patterns include harsh corrections or misapplied aids that aggravate vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises in the paces and their uses (walk, trot, canter, gallop)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedicated instruction for 'EXERCISES IN THE PACES' and separate sections for THE WALK, THE TROT, THE CANTER, THE GALLOP: implies systematic exercises to train horse and rider in each pace, with emphasis on walk and canter for lady's horse and measured use of trot and gallop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat paces as skills to be trained with specific exercises; use exercises to improve precision, ease, and comfort. Anti-patterns: neglecting pace-specific training or forcing paces unsuited to rider/horse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopping and backing, leaping, and dismounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate sections for STOPPING AND BACKING, LEAPING, DISMOUNTING indicate procedural standards and techniques for these maneuvers: controlled stopping/backing, safe leaping technique (when appropriate), and orderly dismounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each maneuver has a prescribed method (mounting was described in detail) and should be executed with attention to balance, rein control, and assistant/groom duties where applicable. Anti-patterns include abrupt stops, unbalanced leaps, and careless dismounts that risk safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as a governing fashion/etiquette principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity in costume and tack is repeatedly enjoined by fashion and taste: 'All that is gaudy, needless, or even elaborate, is vulgar. Perfect simplicity ... is expected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both an aesthetic rubric and practical guidance: choose minimal, tasteful trappings and dress. Over-decoration is an explicit anti-pattern.
